stories.headline: NFL Week 2 betting guide: Top plays for Sunday afternoon's games
stories.summary: Our experts dive into the odds and player props for Week 2 and offer their betting tips and favorite plays.
stories.byline: Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen
stories.body:
Value is value, no matter where -- or how -- you find it. And that's what we'll aim to do each week in this space: finding betting value.

Ben Solak, Seth Walder and Matt Bowen bring different perspectives into how they approach sports betting. Solak leans on his expertise in player evaluation and the X's and O's to find edges, while Walder relies on statistical models to pick out plus-expected value bets, focusing mainly on defense. Bowen, a former NFL safety, predicts positive matchups and game winners from tape study and his understanding of the league.

From spreads and money lines to totals and defensive player props, a good price might be found anywhere. Results will be tracked throughout the season, with flat one-unit wagers for each listed bet. With that, let's dive into our best bets, favorite defensive props and the top game to bet in Week 1.

Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change.

Jump to:

Bowen's Game of the Week | Solak's plays | Walder's props

Bowen's Game of the Week

Cincinnati Bengals at Houston Texans (-2.5, 46.5)

1 p.m. ET on CBS, Reliant Stadium, Houston

This line has fluctuated but at -2.5, I am all-in. Would I feel the same at -3? I wouldn't love it, but I'd be willing to bet Houston at home in a bounce-back game after the Week 1 loss to Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills. Let's get into what to look for on both sides of the ball, and we'll finish with some props bets to play.

When Houston has the ball: Houston spent the offseason working on its run game, trading for David Montgomery and adding to the offensive front. And we saw a dedicated effort to run the football in Week 1, as Montgomery had 20 carries, with Woody Marks chipping in with nine. Now, was it super efficient? No. Montgomery averaged just 3.0 YPC, and the Texans registered a run block win rate of 74% (17th in the league). But it's clear that Houston wants the run game to be a foundational element of its offense. This can boost the passing opportunities for quarterback C.J. Stroud, who will see a Bengals defense featuring a rebuilt front anchored by defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II and an underrated secondary that can mix both zone and man looks. I would look for play-action concepts (which mirror the run game) to attack the Bengals' two-deep zone shells while also scheming up some shot plays. With Nico Collins out, the scheme won't change in Houston. Xavier Hutchinson and Kayshon Boutte can work the interior in-breakers while Jaylin Noel operates out of the slot. I truly think Houston looks to control the tempo on offense in this one, but let's keep an eye on third downs because the Texans need to beat man coverage from the Bengals there.

When Cincinnati has the ball: I want to see this matchup against the Texans' defense. Though the Bengals looked flat in a Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (Joe Burrow finished with 254 yards passing, and Ja'Marr Chase had two receptions for 12 yards), they create conflict because of scheme and talent. The Texans have been a zone-heavy defense under DeMeco Ryans, but they will mix in man coverage (based on game situations), which creates must-see TV when corners Derek Stingley Jr. and Kamari Lassiter match against Chase and Tee Higgins. Tight end Mike Gesicki (78 yards receiving in Week 1) could find room to operate against Houston's split-safety and single-high zone schemes to attack the voids there. But, my main question is will the Bengals' offensive line keep the pocket firm for Burrow and generate movement up front in the run game? The Bengals held a pass block win rate of 53.8% in Week 1 against the Bucs (13th in the league), while Chase Brown averaged only 3.5 YPC. It's a different matchup this week against Houston edge rushers Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter. Burrow will need to hit some explosive play throws to win this one.

Leans: Texans -2.5 (-118), Texans moneyline (-142), Over 46.5 (-105)

Now, let's get to some prop bets ...

Ja'Marr Chase receptions OVER 6.5 (-109)

I expect a dedicated effort to get Chase the ball after he caught only two of four targets in the Week 1 win over the Bucs -- screens, unders and quicks that cater to Chase's explosive catch-and-run ability. Look for Chase to be involved early in this game plan.

Mike Gesicki anytime TD (+280)

Gesicki caught a Week 1 touchdown on a schemed throw to beat man coverage. Plus, the Bengals can set up Gesicki on zone beaters in the high red zone (seams, corners) to counter the Houston defensive tendencies.

Chase Brown receiving yards OVER 20.5 (-113)

Brown caught five of six targets for 22 yards last week versus Tampa, and the screen game/swing routes could be an early answer to counter the Texans' pass rush.

Solak's plays

Green Bay Packers -3.5 (-112) at New York Jets

I'm grabbing a quick buy-low spot on the Packers, who were much better Sunday than the box score would indicate. The Minnesota Vikings scored 14 late points on defensive takeaways deep in Green Bay territory in their 39-22 victory. But the Packers had a better success rate (38.8%) than the Vikings (34.5%) and struggled only in situational spots. They were 3-for-12 on third down. On four red zone trips, they scored only one touchdown and one field goal. Those are the little execution problems that hurt a box score.

Going from facing a Brian Flores-coached Vikings defense to the Jets should make things far easier. Matt LaFleur has experience facing Aaron Glenn from when Glenn was the defensive coordinator of the Detroit Lions and generally has found success (46% offensive success rate, 0.04 EPA per play, 2.2 points per drive).

I thought about taking the Packers' team total, currently priced at 23.5 and juiced -135 to the over. I think the Jets' offense will be a functional group this season, but they need to run the ball and play clock control to win games against superior opponents -- and that might limit the Packers' total drives. As such, I'll go instead for the full-game spread at -3.5. I would play this no further than -120.

Tennessee Titans team total UNDER 15.5 (-105)

The Titans' offensive operation was the worst I saw in Week 1: play designs that were dead in the water, offensive linemen uncertain of their assignments, easy drops and bad routes from receivers and poor accuracy and timing from Cam Ward at quarterback. It's tough to find anything to hang their hat on from a 23-10 loss to the Jets.

It's worth remarking that Brian Daboll's offenses have been poor in Week 1 -- six, six and and zero points in the three seasons previous -- and then stronger in Week 2. But against this Philadelphia Eagles defense, it's tough to have much faith. Philadelphia's defensive front looked as deep and disruptive as ever against an average Washington Commanders front, and the Titans are comfortably one of the eight worst lines in football. Though defensive back Cooper DeJean was banged up in the Week 1 game and sat out practice Wednesday, the Eagles' outside corner duo of Quinyon Mitchell and Riq Woolen still poses a huge problem for the Titans' ability to create explosive plays through the air.

The talent difference here feels simply insurmountable. The Titans will need defensive takeaways or big special teams outputs to get into scoring range. I don't see them getting enough. I would play this up to -115.

New England Patriots -5.5 (-105) vs. Pittsburgh Steelers

The past four defenses the Patriots have faced are as follows: Seattle Seahawks (Week 1), Seahawks (Super Bowl), Denver Broncos (AFC Championship Game), Houston Texans (AFC divisional round). Even their wild-card opponent had a near-elite defense (Los Angeles Chargers). We are finally at a point at which we can buy low on the Patriots against an imperfect defense.

The Pittsburgh Steelers' defense was hardly tested in Week 1 against the Cooper Rush-led Atlanta Falcons. Drake Maye and the Patriots' offense -- especially with TreVeyon Henderson returning from a right ankle injury -- represent a far stiffer test. Even though wide receiver A.J. Brown is on injured reserve because of an ankle injury, the Patriots have had a long week since last Wednesday to prepare for his absence. Their wide receiver room, featuring Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Mack Hollins, is plenty deep enough.

On the other side of the ball, Pittsburgh's offense was dreadful against a Falcons defense that was low in my power ratings to start the season. The Steelers' 31.4% success rate was the worst of all offenses in Week 1, and their 4.1 yards per play was fourth worst. There were some drops and procedural issues that made the performance look worse than it was, but it wasn't a good outing. I like the Patriots' corners and their ability to press Pittsburgh's receivers, forcing Aaron Rodgers into low-percentage prayers while the elite defensive tackle duo of Milton Williams and Christian Barmore generate TFLs and sacks.

This number has been rising throughout the week. I wouldn't play -5.5 at anything past -110.

Lamar Jackson rushing yards UNDER 39.5 (-112)

Jackson's rushing under was a common bet for us throughout last season, when it was clear that the Ravens' quarterback was not healthy. He is healthy this season, as 16-yard and 19-yard scrambles in Week 1 against the Indianapolis Colts indicate. Jackson ended the day with 40 rushing yards on seven carries (after losing three yards on three kneels).

New offensive coordinator Declan Doyle put Jackson under center more than Todd Monken and Greg Roman had previously. Under-center alignments limit the opportunity for designed QB run plays, like read-options. Jackson's lone designed carry against the Colts was a second-and-goal play from the 5-yard line. Though Jackson is still dangerous on a scramble, if he's only going to get designed carries in short-yardage or goal-line situations, his potential for high-yardage days will be capped.

I expect the New Orleans Saints and Brandon Staley's zone-heavy defense to keep much better eyes on Jackson in the scramble drill than the Colts' man-heavy approach afforded. I'll also be looking for an under on Jackson's longest rush when that line posts, but I'd take this number down to 37.5.

KC Concepcion receiving yards OVER 31.5 (-111)

Let's posit rather safely that the Cleveland Browns will be in trailing game scripts for most of their contests against functional teams. While trailing the Jacksonville Jaguars mightily in Week 1, Concepcion ran only 17 routes, below that of fellow rookie Denzel Boston (26) and veteran Jerry Jeudy (22). But Concepcion was targeted on 29.4% of his routes, well above Jeudy and Boston's numbers. He got easy targets too -- a screen, a checkdown -- that create reliable opportunity. But 47.1% of his routes went vertical -- again, higher than Boston or Jeudy -- which indicates the Browns want to get him more opportunity downfield. I expect Concpecion's role to only grow in the offense week over week, and I like his potential both for high-volume YAC days and big downfield splashes.

Aaron Jones Sr. rushing attempts OVER 15.5 (-101)

The Minnesota Vikings' offense has hit an immediate state of disarray with the concussion to QB Kyler Murray (questionable for Week 2) and the injured reserve stint for RB Jordan Mason (thumb). If Murray can't go and Carson Wentz plays, I expect the Vikings to be fairly run-heavy to shorten the game and keep the Chicago Bears offense on the opposing sideline. Without Mason, that means plenty of carries for Jones.

If Murray can go, I still think we'll see the Vikings deploy the new-look running game they were excited about all offseason, yet barely got to utilize given Murray's early injury in Week 1. Veteran DeeJay Dallas and rookie Demond Claiborne are both rostered behind Jones, but it's hard to imagine either biting that much into Jones' share of carries; Dallas is a classic third-down back, and Claiborne was inactive in Week 1. I'll be looking to take Jones' rushing yards up to some alts (70+ and 80+) if Murray is confirmed out before kickoff.

Walder's prop bets

Note: More defensive props will be added as odds become available

Defensive plays

Chicago Bears D/ST anytime touchdown (+750)

One medium good game from Carson Wentz should not make us forget about the fact that he is still Carson Wentz, a QB plenty prone to mistakes. Certainly my model hasn't, which is one reason why it likes Chicago's defense -- which is probably not a great unit overall -- or its special teams' chances to return a touchdown. The fact that the Bears have a prolific offense and are more likely to be in the lead in this game -- thus forcing the Minnesota Vikings to put the ball in Wentz's hands -- helps. I'd bet this down to +700.

Carolina Panthers D/ST anytime touchdown (+700)

As of this writing, we don't know who the Atlanta Falcons' quarterback will be Sunday. Guess what? They're all great options ... for the Panthers' defense. We're betting on a defensive or special teams score against:

A banged-up Cooper Rush or
A banged-up Tua Tagovailoa or
Michael Penix Jr., in his first start back after ACL surgery, or
Jack Strand

No matter what we think of the Panthers' defense, we should take this bet at +700. I would bet it down to +640.

Boye Mafe over 0.25 sacks (+240)

Mafe was a pass rush win rate darling in Seattle and finished ninth-best in the metric at edge last season despite recording just 2.0 sacks on the season. That alone would have made him a likely candidate to be underrated in terms of his ability to get sacks heading into 2026, but we have even more working in our favor here. Because now that he's a Bengal Mafe's playing time has increased substantially. Mafe rushed the passer on 73% of clear passing situations in Week 1 up substantially from 44% a year ago. His chances of sacking C.J. Stroud are better than the odds indicate. I would bet this down to +195.

Jared Verse over 0.25 sacks (+175)

The Browns defense was a mess in Week 1 against Jacksonville. And zero pressures and zero sacks from Verse wasn't a great start to his Browns tenure, either. But one game shouldn't override what we know about Verse's quality. Though overlooked as the player going back to the Browns in the Myles Garrett trade, Verse is still a borderline top-10 edge rusher who can stop the run and get after the quarterback. And one game isn't moving me off that stance from a sack forecasting perspective -- especially because the Browns had him on the field on 86% of clear passing situations. Even as heavy underdogs against the Buccaneers, my sacks model says this price is too good to pass up. I would bet this down to +145.

Other sack bets I recommend:

Derrick Brown under 0.25 sacks (-211)

Alex Highsmith over 0.25 sacks (+122)

Devonte Wyatt under 0.25 sacks (-227)

Kenny Clark under 0.25 sacks (-189)

Zach Sieler under 0.25 sacks (-199)

Travon Walker under 0.25 sacks (-158)

Josh Sweat over 0.25 sacks (+148)

Arden Key over 0.25 sacks (+194)

Chris Jones under 0.25 sacks (-167)

Kevin Byard under 6.5 tackles + assists (-115)

Let's start with the simple: last season: dating back to the start of last season, Byard has gone over 6.5 tackles + assists in five of 18 games. That alone doesn't mean we have to bet the under, but it's certainly a useful starting place. It is relevant that in New England, at least last week, Byard played a half yard closer to the line of scrimmage on average and his rate of plays as a box safety increased from 8% to 15%. And he posted a really strong 20% tackle rate against the run (compared to 13% last game). But is that a big enough difference to sway us off the under? I think not. It's a mild change. And then there's this: the Steelers were the No. 1 team in pass rate over expected last week, per NFL Next Gen Stats. If they continue their pass happy ways then the under looks really favorable. I would bet this to -130.

Antonio Johnson over 3.5 tackles + assists (-113)

Here's the most important number you need to know for this bet: last year Johnson played 60% of defensive snaps, in part because he didn't because a starter until halfway through the season. But in his lone game this year he played 88% of the snaps. And I'm not sure the playing time change has been fully baked in. Yes, Johnson is a low-tackling safety: since the start of 2025 he ranks in the 26th percentile in tackle rate and just the 8th percentile on run plays. But that's largely overridden by the fact that he looks to be a nearly every-play safety for the Jaguars. From the time I wrote this prop up to when I filed it, the odds moved substantially. I would still bet it at this price, but I wouldn't if the odds move further.

Other tackle bets I recommend:

Quinnen Williams under 4.5 tackles + assists (-155)

Josh Hines-Allen under 3.5 tackles + assists (-102)

Offensive plays

Aaron Rodgers pass attempts UNDER 35.5 (-124)

That the Pittsburgh Steelers were the No. 1 team in pass rate over expectation in Week 1, per NFL Next Gen Stats, was arguably more of an upset than the Los Angeles Chargers losing to the Arizona Cardinals. Will it continue? I'm willing to bet it won't, at least for this week. Mike McCarthy has had both pass-leaning and run-leaning teams in the past, but he also doesn't have a particularly good quarterback right now, so it hardly seems to make sense that they would keep up the pattern. That's why I'm agreeing with my pass attempts model, which thinks this line is too high for Rodgers, even heading into a game in which the Steelers are underdogs and will have to keep up with the New England Patriots' offense. I would bet this down to -150.

Rhamondre Stevenson receptions OVER 2.5 (-153)

The entire league ran zone coverage at a higher rate in Week 1 than in any season in our dataset (since 2017), but no team epitomized that more than the Steelers. Under coordinator Patrick Graham, the Steelers ran zone 89% of the time. Why does that matter for this bet? Since 2023, running backs have caught passes on man-coverage plays 8% of the time but 15% of the time against zone. That massive disparity plays into our hands here with Stevenson facing the Steelers. I opted for the conservative option at over 2.5, but I don't mind betting the longer-odds alts on this, either.

Malik Willis 24+ completions (+910)

I thought there was a chance the Miami Dolphins would go run-heavy to the extreme with their offense, but in Week 1 it was more of a normal split than I was expecting. Malik Willis threw 27 passes, and the Dolphins ranked 11th in pass rate over expected. My attempts model sees value in the extreme tail outcome here, and I don't think it's that hard to imagine. If the Dolphins fall way behind in this game -- and I suspect they will against the 49ers -- they'll be forced to pass and pass and pass. And there also might be plenty of short throws available for Willis to make. I like this long shot.

stories.headline: Acuña grand slam leads Braves to 6-3 win, dropping Astros from AL West lead
stories.summary: — Ronald Acuña Jr. hit a go-ahead grand slam in the seventh inning, and the Atlanta Braves beat Houston 6-3 Saturday night to drop the Astros out of the AL West lead.
stories.body:
HOUSTON -- — Ronald Acuña Jr. hit a go-ahead grand slam in the seventh inning, and the Atlanta Braves beat Houston 6-3 Saturday night to drop the Astros out of the AL West lead.


Houston (77-78) fell one game behind Texas (78-77) and trails the Chicago White Sox (79-76) by two games for the last AL wild card. The Astros had held at least a share of the division lead each day since Aug. 25.


Atlanta assured its eighth playoff berth in nine seasons on Friday and is in position to clinch its first NL East title since 2023 on Sunday.


Trailing 2-1, Atlanta loaded the bases against AJ Blubaugh (5-3) and Acuña homered off Bryan Abreu for his second grand slam this season and the fifth of his big league career.


Acuña singled and walked twice in his first three plate appearances. He has homered in three of his last four games.


Mike Yastrzemski added a solo homer in the eighth inning.


Grant Holmes (10-5) allowed two runs and eight hits over six innings.


Yainer Diaz hit an RBI double in the eighth off Dylan Lee, who struck out pinch-hitter Nelson Velázquez to end the inning.


Raisel Iglesias pitched a perfect ninth inning for his 34th save in 37 chances.


Jose Altuve had three hits for Houston, while Isaac Paredes was 2 for 3 with a home run, walk and two RBI.


Christian Walker had two hits after entering the game hitless in his previous 23 at-bats.


Hayden Wesneski allowed one run on four hits over 5 1/3 innings.


Up next
Astros RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.43 ERA) and Braves LHP Martín Pérez (9-9, 3.07 ERA) start Sunday.

stories.headline: UFC 331: Live results and analysis for Van vs. Pantoja 2
stories.summary: Follow as Alexandre Pantoja attempts to reclaim the flyweight title against Joshua Van at UFC 331.
stories.body:
The men's flyweight division takes center stage Saturday night. Former champion Alexandre Pantoja returns from a nine-month layoff to challenge champion Joshua Van in a main event rematch at UFC 331 at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. The main card begins at 9 p.m. ET.

Pantoja, ESPN's No. 8-ranked pound-for-pound fighter, suffered a dislocated elbow in the opening seconds of his first fight against Van at UFC 323 in December, giving Van the TKO win and the men's flyweight title. While Pantoja recovered from injury, Van defended the belt against Tatsuro Taira, earning a fifth-round knockout at UFC 328 in May.

Top-10 lightweights Arman Tsarukyan and Mauricio Ruffy meet in the co-main event. Tsarukyan hasn't been in the Octagon since November 2025, but don't expect him to be rusty. One of the promotion's best grapplers has stayed sharp in competitive wrestling matches with RAF and has become a fan favorite on social media. Ruffy, meanwhile, has made a career out of knocking opponents out. Thirteen of his 14 career wins have come via KO, including his two 2026 fights against Rafael Fiziev and Michael Chandler.

Brett Okamoto, Jeff Wagenheim and Dre Waters break down all the action from Los Angeles.

stories.headline: Hawks and their fans rage after devastating AFL loss
stories.summary: Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell spoke of mourning after they lost an epic AFL preliminary final, with a controversial umpiring decision pivotal at the end.
stories.body:
The biggest noise immediately after one of the all-time greatest AFL games was the booing, which was venal in its fury.

Hawthorn players James Sicily, Tom Barrass and Jack Ginnivan had angry words with the umpires, who then had bottles thrown at them from Hawks fans as they left the MCG on Saturday night.

Ruckman Lloyd Meek swore as he spoke to reporters in the rooms. Coach Sam Mitchell impressively kept his emotions in check throughout a fraught post-game media conference, where he spoke of mourning.

"This feeling is the pits," Mitchell said.

At the heart of Hawthorn's collective rage was the holding-the-ball free paid against Jarman Impey in the last minute of an epic preliminary final. It was the most controversial of a succession of contentious umpiring calls through the game.

Brisbane's Hugh McCluggage then kicked the match-winning goal - the ninth lead-change of the game and the fourth in the last few frenetic minutes.

Mitchell said he did not know about Sicily, Barrass and Ginnivan going to the umpires, but he was aware of the bottles being thrown onto the ground.

"At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears, part of me wanted to scream with rage, part of me wanted to throw chairs, you don't know how to react," he said.

"So when you're in the stand, you need to continue to be feeling that emotion, because that's why we love it, but how it manifests itself - we shouldn't be throwing things on the field and doing those types of things.

"But the passion in the stand and the passion of the game is why we love it so much. So I hope that for the vast majority it was felt responsibly."

Meek was near Impey when the free was paid.

"It's heartbreaking ... excuse the profanity, you can edit that one out. We pour our heart and soul into this," Meek said.

"I was standing right next to him - I will be replaying that one for a while.

"I just feel like I probably could have jumped on and knocked the ball out or done a 'stacks-on' - something ... it's hard, in the dying moments."

Mitchell spoke of grief and added it was too soon to think beyond what had just happened.

"I think we're in a mourning phase. What's the first part, is it anger? I think I'm still half in anger, probably sense it in my body language," he said.

"What else, what's after anger? I don't know, last is acceptance and - I nearly said a bad word - I'm a long way from acceptance right now.

"I will sit in anger for a bit longer, I'm sure all the players will too."

Before they left the MCG for the last time this season, Mitchell brought his players into a tight group.

"It was just 'remember this'. There's nothing more raw than that five minutes straight after the siren, when it hurts the most," Meek said of Mitchell's message.

"Remember the burn and the outrage and how frustrating it is - because that will be our fuel. We have a big pre-season ahead."

Mitchell spoke of his great pride in the Hawks, who staged an outstanding comeback in the final quarter.

But in the end, it came to nothing.

"If you want to strive for great things, you will open yourself up for all sorts of emotion, the greatest of joy, and the deepest of pain," he said.

stories.headline: Teenager Julian Hall scores lone goal in Red Bulls' victory over NYCFC
stories.summary: Julian Hall scored early in the second half and keeper Ethan Horvath was never tested for the New York Red Bulls in a 1-0 victory over New York City FC on Friday night at Yankee Stadium.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- Julian Hall scored early in the second half and keeper Ethan Horvath was never tested for the New York Red Bulls in a 1-0 victory over New York City FC on Friday night at Yankee Stadium.

Hall scored unassisted in the 57th minute for his 10th goal this season. The 18-year-old forward scored three times in his first 38 appearances.

Horvath did not have to make a save for the Red Bulls (9-11-6). It was his fourth clean sheet in 26 starts in his first season in the league.

Matt Freese totaled four saves for NYCFC (8-10-8), which falls to 4-6-4 at home. He had the lone save in the scoreless first half.

The Red Bulls have won two straight following a six-match winless streak, improving to 5-6-3 away from home after a four-match trip.

NYCFC was coming off a 2-0 road win over Real Salt Lake that snapped a seven-match winless stretch.

The two clubs played to a 1-1 draw at Red Bull Arena in May.

The Red Bulls lead the all-time series in all competitions 17-13-5 and they are 2-1-1 in their last four trips to Yankee Stadium.

Up next New York: Hosts St. Louis City on Sept. 26.

New York City: At Atlanta United on Sept. 26.

stories.headline: Azerbaijan Grand Prix 2026: Race start time in Baku, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1 is heading to the streets of Baku for this year's Azerbaijan Grand Prix as we roll into the business end of the season.
stories.body:
Formula 1 is heading to the streets of Baku for this year's Azerbaijan Grand Prix as we roll into the business end of the season.

Title leader Kimi Antonelli extended his lead in the drivers' championship after picking up his eighth victory of the season at the brand-new Madring last time out.

He leads his teammate George Russell by 81 points, with Lewis Hamilton now dropping back in the title race after a retirement in Spain.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 15th race of the season.

- Madring's F1 debut left everyone dissatisfied, even Spanish GP's top 3

- Max Verstappen wins Max vs 100 in style after overtaking 100 go-karters in 35 minutes

- F1 2027 calendar: Monaco GP gets sprint race, Türkiye and Portugal return to schedule

Azerbaijan Grand Prix schedule
All times in BST

Thursday, September 24

Practice One: 9.30 a.m. - 10.30 a.m.

Practice Two: 1 p.m. - 2 p.m.

Friday, September 25

Final Practice: 9.30 a.m. - 10.30 a.m.

Qualifying: 1 p.m. - 2 p.m.

Saturday, September 26

Azerbaijan Grand Prix: 12 p.m.

How to watch

Sky Sports has exclusive F1 rights again in 2026 in the U.K., with every session live on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Azerbaijan Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Why is the race on a Saturday?
For the first time in Baku's history, the F1 weekend will shift a day forwards, with the race taking place on a Saturday to avoid a clash with an Azerbaijan National Day of mourning on the Sunday.

Azerbaijan's people will dedicate their thoughts to military personnel and those who died during the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War.

Baku City Circuit

After the European leg of the calendar where circuits are more traditional, Baku is one of the standout street circuits of the season.

The first race in Baku was held in 2016 as the European Grand Prix before it was called the Azerbaijan Grand Prix a year later.

The section around Turns 8, 9 and 10 are lined by the walls of the city's charming old town including a castle and the long main straight along the Baku shoreline sees cars reach speeds in excess of 220 mph and is the best spot for overtaking.

The walls are narrow and the high-speeds make for either a race full of chaos, or none at all. There is a 57% chance of a Safety Car being deployed during the race.

Azerbaijan Grand Prix

Circuit: Baku City Circuit; Baku, Azerbaijan

Previous winners
2016: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2017: Daniel Ricciardo (Red Bull)

2018: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2019: Valtteri Bottas (Mercedes)

2021: Sergio Pérez (Red Bull)

2022: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

2023: Sergio Pérez (Red Bull)

2024: Oscar Piastri (McLaren)

2025: Max Verstappen (Red Bull)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2016 European GP. (First race as Azerbaijan GP in 2017)

Laps: 51 laps of 6km.

Lap record: 1:43.009, Charles Leclerc (2019).

Most wins: Pérez (2021, 2023) and Verstappen (2022, 2025) with two wins each. Other winners from the current grid are Hamilton (2018), Bottas (2019) and Piastri (2024).

Most poles: Leclerc with four (2021-2024) and Hamilton (2017), Bottas (2019) and Verstappen (2025) are the other pole sitters from the current grid.

Weather forecast

The weather for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix will be dry and sunny throughout the weekend. Temperatures will be around 26°C, but will drop to 24°C for the race on Saturday.

What happened last year?
Red Bull's Verstappen took pole position around the streets of Baku in a qualifying session that featured a record six red flags.

He ended up converting that pole into a dominant victory, with Russell in second and Carlos Sainz behind.

It was a key moment in the championship fight between Lando Norris and Piastri as Norris closed the gap to 25 points to his McLaren teammate after the Australian crashed out.

Who will win this year?

The last street circuit this year was in Monaco in June and since then several of the top teams have upgraded its packages and haven't yet gone racing on street circuits, but Baku has now arrived.

Antonelli has looked on fire in the last two races, but Norris is creeping to the front. The reigning world champion has two wins to his name in Hungary and Zandvoort, but also suffered an unlucky run in Madrid with the safety car deployment, so missed out on a potential win there as well.

Mercedes are set to be quick in the high-speed straight lines in Baku, but the tight and twisty corners might suit Ferrari and McLaren best.

One of the main aims will be to not crash the car into the wall otherwise the whole course of the race can rapidly change in a blink of an eye.

stories.headline: Still at zero: Viral Man United fan's haircut challenge nears two years
stories.summary: Viral Manchester United fan Frank Ilett's haircut challenge is nearing the two-year mark and he's back to square 1.
stories.body:
For most clubs, failure or success can be defined in points, trophies and medals. Manchester United are the same, but they can also define it in days. More specifically, it can be summed up in 712 days.

That's how long viral United fan Frank Ilett, also known as The United Strand, has gone without a haircut as he waits for the team to win five games in a row.

After finishing last season with wins over Nottingham Forest and Brighton, Michael Carrick's side could have completed the job with wins over newly promoted Hull City and Ipswich Town before finishing with a win away at Everton. As it turned out, that's not at all what happened.

An embarrassing 2-0 away defeat to Hull meant going back to square one. A 5-2 win over Ipswich might have promoted hopes that the season opener was just an unwanted blip, but a draw to Everton and a controversial defeat to 10-man Manchester City poured further cold water.

How could it get worse? Well, a 2-0 lead inside the first 10 minutes against Brighton in the Carabao Cup ended in a surprise 3-2 defeat.

Left watching on, his hair growing ever longer, is Ilett. His challenge will now officially reach the two-year mark -- his last haircut was on Oct. 5, 2024 -- and his hair is now almost 14 inches at its longest point.

In the meantime, Ilett continues to raise money for the Little Princess Trust, which creates wigs for children with cancer.

The only thing that can happen now before Ilett soars past two years is for United to win away to Fulham in their last game before the international break.

stories.headline: Sharks dismiss rebuild theory amid fresh finals pain
stories.summary: Cronulla are adamant they will be in the fight for the NRL premiership in 2027 despite undergoing an off-season roster overhaul.
stories.body:
Craig Fitzgibbon insists Cronulla won't be entering a rebuild phase as the Sharks prepare to undergo one of the most significant off-season shake-ups of the coach's tenure.

After Nicho Hynes was concussed in the opening stages of Saturday's semi-final to the Sydney Roosters, the Sharks fought on bravely before being overrun in a 46-10 defeat.

Cronulla have made the finals every year since Fitzgibbon took charge in 2022 but have yet to make the grand final.

"There's only been two teams that have won the comp in the last five years," Fitzgibbon said.

"We're not that far off, but we haven't got there.

"So that's a fair criticism and it's frustrating, but we haven't got there.

"We've got to work out how and what we do with what we've got to get there."

Seven players will move to new clubs over the off-season, including a quartet who have been ever present under Fitzgibbon -- lock Cameron McInnes (York), Siosifa Talakai (Perth) and the North Queensland-bound duo of Sione Katoa and Jesse Ramien.

"We've been up for five years now with the same group of guys, and a portion of those are leaving, and we'll be forever grateful for their service," Fitzgibbon said.

"We've punched above our weight for a long time now.

"It won't be hard to replace them. Everyone thinks we'll need a reset, rebuild but no, we'll just keep going.

"We've got some guys ready to go, we won't be going anywhere."

Hynes' exclusion after failing his head injury assessment set the wheels in motion for another finals defeat for the Sharks, who now boast a 4-7 post-season record under Fitzgibbon.

Halfback Hynes has frequently been the target for criticism when Cronulla have fallen short in September.

But the No.7 was quick to apologise to his teammates after he got his head on the wrong side in a tackle on Salesi Foketi.

"He went out there and went head first for the first collision he could get and the timing was wrong, but it's just a sign of how much he wanted it," Fitzgibbon added.

"It cost him dearly but he just apologised. He knows that he had a moment that he had an opportunity for tonight which was important to him and us.

"It went wrong, but you can handle that when you go in head first and you're committed for the team."

stories.headline: Charles scores 16 as Valkyries conclude regular-season home schedule with 70-57 win over Seattle
stories.summary: — Kaila Charles had 16 points and matched her career high with 12 rebounds, Tiffany Hayes scored 10 points a night before her 37th birthday, and the Golden State Valkyries concluded their regular-season home schedule by beating the Seattle Storm 70-57...
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- — Kaila Charles had 16 points and matched her career high with 12 rebounds, Tiffany Hayes scored 10 points a night before her 37th birthday, and the Golden State Valkyries concluded their regular-season home schedule by beating the Seattle Storm 70-57 on Saturday night for a sixth straight win.


Rookie Juste Jocyte and Laeticia Amihere each added 11 points off the bench for the Valkyries (31-11), who are in second place behind Minnesota.


The Valkyries wrapped up a 17-5 home record with another sold-out crowd of 18,064, bringing the second-season attendance total to 397,408 — with a full house for every game at Chase Center over a second straight year.


It’s the only franchise in WNBA history to sell out every home game over its first two seasons.


Seattle (8-34), finishing up one of the worst seasons in team history, lost its third in a row and sixth of seven. Rookie Flau'jae Johnson had 17 points to lead the Storm.


Golden State coach Natalie Nakase again rested her stars who are just back from the FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup.


The Valkyries again were without star Gabby Williams and top reserve Janelle Salaun, both of whom played for the French team that lost to the U.S. 97-79 in the World Cup final on Sunday in Berlin. Nakase was an assistant for the U.S.


Valkyries forward Cecilia Zandalasini also sat out again Saturday with an illness after she played for Italy in the World Cup.


Golden State missed six of its first seven 3-point tries and wound up 9 for 26 from long range. Kayla Thornton finished the game 0 of 6, including four 3s, but grabbed six rebounds.


Up next
Storm: Visit Las Vegas on Sunday to complete a road back-to-back.


Valkyries: Visit Portland on Tuesday night.

stories.headline: Rangers take sole possession of AL West lead, Quantrill leaves with injury in 6-3 win over Blue Jays
stories.summary: — Five relievers held Toronto to six hits after Cal Quantrill left 12 pitches in because of right lat tightness, and the Rangers moved into sole possession of the AL West lead for the first time since late August with a 6-2 win over the Blue Jays on...
stories.body:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- — Five relievers held Toronto to six hits after Cal Quantrill left 12 pitches in because of right lat tightness, and the Rangers moved into sole possession of the AL West lead for the first time since late August with a 6-2 win over the Blue Jays on Saturday night.


Texas (78-77) has won six of seven and moved a half-game ahead of Houston (77-78), which holds the tiebreaker. The Rangers have a winning record for the first time since before play on Aug. 11.


Jordan Montgomery (1-0) got his first win since Aug. 14, 2024, pitching 3 2/3 hitless innings. He returned from Tommy John surgery this past Aug. 9.


Davis Schneider hit a pinch-homer for the AL champion Blue Jays (76-79), who have lost eight of 12. They trail the Chicago White Sox by three games for the AL’s final wild card.


Quantrill a, son former Toronto All-Star Paul Quantrill, retired George Springer on a groundout opening the second inning and didn’t appear to exhibit any pain but didn’t face another batter. The 31-year-old right-hander left his previous start on Sept. 13 at Arizona after 70 pitches because of a sore back.


Rangers manager Skip Schumaker said after the game he had no update on Quantrill, who is to have an MRI on Sunday.


Quantrill was followed by Montgomery, and Nathan Eovaldi, Robert Garcia, Chase Silseth and Jacob Latz pitched one inning each.


Texas scored twice in the second off José Soriano (12-8) without a base hit, helped by a walk, hit batter, infield throwing error and a wild pitch.


Texas’ three-run sixth featured an RBI double by Wyatt Langford when left fielder Myles Straw pulled up as the ball land between him and the wall.


Soriano allowed six runs — five earned — pitching three batters into the sixth.


UP NEXT


Rangers RHP Jacob deGrom (11-9, 3.79), who is 8-2 at home this season with a .183 opponents batting average, starts Sunday while the Blue Jays employ a bullpen game.

stories.headline: Conor McGregor expected to fight in bare-knuckle once UFC deal expires
stories.summary: David Feldman, founder of the Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship (BKFC), told ESPN he would "bet everything" that Conor McGregor fights for the promotion once his UFC contract expires.
stories.body:
Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship (BKFC) founder David Feldman told ESPN he would "bet everything" that Conor McGregor fights for the promotion once his UFC contract expires.

McGregor returned to the Octagon in July following a five-year hiatus from the sport, losing to Max Holloway in the first round after sustaining a knee injury in the opening seconds of the fight.

The former two-weight world champion is also a partner in BKFC, which was founded by Feldman in 2018, and has one fight left on his UFC contract.

McGregor, 38, became a part owner of the bare-knuckle promotion in 2024 and is now expected to compete in the sport once his deal with the UFC expires.

"He has one fight left with UFC, when that fight is done I would bet everything that he will be fighting for BKFC," Feldman told ESPN.

"I'm definitely enthused by his enthusiasm. I didn't think we were going to get this out of him. I didn't think he was going to fall in love with the sport as much as he did.

"He's one of the biggest fans in BKFC, not just a partner. He says some really critical things that help us promote the fighters and do different things."

In the days after his short-lived return to UFC, McGregor confirmed he would have surgery on his ACL but hinted he could fight again in summer 2027.

Feldman said the Irishman is heavily involved with the business side of BKFC and expects his focus to shift to the sport fully once his UFC career is done.

"We listen to a lot of the different suggestions he has in building stars but he's been fantastic, he's jumping on board now since he started to recover from his injury," Feldman said.

"Obviously he's going to take another hiatus when he trains for his next UFC fight and then it's all BKFC."

BKFC will host its next event in Manchester, England, on Sept. 26, with Darren Till facing fellow former UFC star Yoel Romero.

stories.headline: Brisbane Lions make fourth-straight Grand Final in incredible MCG scenes
stories.summary: Brisbane have survived an almighty final-quarter fightback from Hawthorn to win an all-time great AFL preliminary final by nine points.
stories.body:
Brisbane will face Fremantle for a shot at a premiership "three-peat" after surviving an almighty last-quarter fightback from Hawthorn to win an all-time great and controversial AFL preliminary final by nine points.

A contentious holding-the-ball decision against Hawks defender Jarman Impey gave Hugh McCluggage a free kick and he kicked the match-deciding goal with 18 seconds left.

Brisbane then won the centre bounce and Kai Lohmann kicked another goal on the siren to seal a nine-point win, 20.11 (131) to 19.8 (122), in front of 97,835 fans at the MCG on Saturday.

"Has there ever been a more exciting game of AFL football than that one?" Lions coach Chris Fagan said.

"If I was a spectator, I'd just be rapt by that.

"Hawthorn are unlucky, no team deserved to lose tonight.

"We're just lucky enough that we were in front when the siren went and we get to fight another day."

The Lions are aiming to become the third team this century - Brisbane in 2001-03 and Hawthorn in 2013-15 - to pull off a three-peat when they meet Fremantle in a final for the first time next Saturday.

But after losing one of the AFL's greatest ever games, Hawthorn will seethe over the Impey decision, which prompted co-captain James Sicily and defender Tom Barrass to blast the umpires.

"I don't think anyone's going to be sleeping that well tonight after how that last goal went down," Barrass told the Seven Network.

Hawks fans were in uproar after the final siren and a bottle was thrown at the umpires as they left the field, after their team had rallied from 28 points behind during the last quarter.

Hawks coach Sam Mitchell took more issue with preceding calls - a high free kick paid to Dayne Zorko, and another where forward Mitch Lewis was penalised for showing "insufficient intent" to keep the ball in play.

Asked if the Impey call was a free kick, Mitchell said: "I haven't rewatched it. Maybe.

"There were a few. It's probably not the one I was focused on - a couple that led up to it and some key moments in the game.

"I'm sure the umpires will assess how they performed in that game, in key moments - the Mitch Lewis out-of-bounds one and the Zorko free kick, but not for me to say."

Fagan believed the Impey free kick was there.

"I didn't necessarily have the greatest of views, but it didn't look like Impey was actually trying to get the ball out," Fagan said.

"I think that's what caused the umpire to pay the free kick."

There were nine lead changes - four alone late in the final term.

Key forward Lewis took a soaring mark and kicked a goal to put Hawthorn back in front late.

Barrass and Sicily then took two massive defensive marks, but the Lions went forward again and the crucial free was paid.

"If you want to strive for great things, you will open yourself up for all sorts of emotion, the greatest of joy, and the deepest of pain," Mitchell said.

"That was a game for the ages. I'm sure I'll appreciate it at some point, but right now I would rather be anywhere but here."

Hawthorn's Nick Watson, dubbed "The Wizard", was best afield with a magical six goals, and was instrumental in their brave last-quarter charge.

Trailing by 22 points in the second term and 16 points in the third, Brisbane went on a scoring rampage that appeared to have decided the game, before Hawthorn's outstanding rally.

McCluggage's ice-cold match-winner capped a 23-disposal, three-goal showing.

Will Ashcroft (28 disposals, eight clearances) and Lachie Neale (26, nine clearances) were strong, and co-captain Harris Andrews cut off multiple Hawthorn attacks.

Fagan said Neale only suffered a hit to the chest, not a head knock, after he was collected by Jai Newcombe in the first minute of the game.

Lohmann (five goals) turned the game with a three-goal third quarter.

Hawks Jack Gunston (five goals) and Lewis (four goals) hit the scoreboard in Hawthorn's highest losing score since 2005, while Josh Ward (11 clearances, 25 disposals) was huge.

stories.headline: 2026 NBA free agency: Grades for offseason signings, extensions
stories.summary: We're grading the biggest free agent signings and extensions, including Keyonte George's extension with the Jazz.
stories.body:
The NBA offseason is here, and teams across the league have been busy making moves. Free agency officially began June 30.

I'm grading every free agent signing and the most impactful extensions this offseason, breaking down the ramifications for all teams and players involved.

To determine each grade, I'm looking at multiple factors, including the player's on-court impact and age, the contract's financial implications and the context of the team's short- and long-term outlooks. How risky or certain is the move? And how much does it help or hurt the team's chance to win a championship, next season or beyond?

Let's get into the latest moves:

Quick links:

Trade grades | Latest buzz | Trade machine

Depth charts | Trade tracker | More coverage

Sept. 18: Heat give Larsson a new deal
Pelle Larsson terms: Four years, $60 million, with a mutual option in the fourth year

Grade: B

At summer league in Las Vegas this year, I had a conversation with various NBA folks about the Miami Heat. We were talking about the Heat's lineup possibilities around Giannis Antetokounmpo and how they might build a winner with depleted depth. One clear conclusion from this conversation was that Pelle Larsson was going to get a lot of minutes because Heat coach Erik Spoelstra adores him.

The 25-year-old Swedish guard was a steal at the No. 44 pick in the 2024 draft, and he took a big step forward last season, averaging 11.4 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.4 assists. The Heat also trust him as a lead defender on the perimeter. He ranked fourth on the team in starts and fifth in total minutes last season.

Larsson profiles as a high-floor, low-ceiling player, given his age and skill set. Most prominently, a shaky 3-point shot (33% in his career) means he's not truly a 3-and-D player but rather a jack of all trades who fits the Heat's preferred ethos with his hustle and stamina.

Still, that high floor means a $15 million average for Larsson is a reasonable value for Miami, and this new deal will carry him through most of his prime years. Larsson must be happy with his new deal, given that his rookie contract was worth only $5.4 million over three years. Spoelstra must be happy to lock up one of his favorite players for the long term, too.

Sept. 18: George, Jazz agree to extension
Keyonte George terms: Five years, $157.5 million

Grade: C+

George was one of the breakout players of the 2025-26 season, averaging 23.6 points and 6.1 assists while making 37% of his 3-pointers. He also boosted his efficiency from 7-8% below average in his first two seasons to 5% above average last year, which made him one of the top offensive guards in the sport.

On its own, that trajectory -- combined with George's age, as he'll turn 23 in November -- makes him more than worthy of this new rookie extension, which will pay him an average of $31.5 million per year. For context, this contract will pay nearly $100 million less over half a decade compared with the possible 25% max (which Victor Wembanyama, another member of the 2023 draft class, signed earlier this offseason).

But the complication with analyzing George's new deal is uncertainty about his ability on the other end. The Jazz have been worse with George on the floor versus when he's off in every season of his career to date. The defensive swing has been particularly problematic: Per Cleaning the Glass, Utah's defensive rating was 6.7 points worse with George last season and 8.7 points worse in 2024-25. Both marks ranked in the bottom 10% of players leaguewide.

Because of that track record, advanced stats that factor in on/off data are much lower in their assessment of George than his shiny box score stats would suggest. DARKO rates George as the third-least-valuable defender in the league, and both estimated plus-minus and xRAPM put him all the way in last place. Other players in his range include the likes of Cam Thomas and Trae Young, who have proved difficult to build around because of their limitations.

It's possible that this indictment of George is attributable to Utah's noncompetitive status during his time there; the Jazz haven't exactly been concerned about finishing 30th, 29th and 29th on defense over the past three years, as they've sought high draft picks instead of regular-season wins. Perhaps in a more competitive situation going forward, George will prove himself a mediocre or even normally below-average defender, rather than the truly terrible defender that his current metrics suggest.

But it's impossible to know that yet, so this grade comes in lower than what might be expected for a rising young star signing a reasonable-looking contract. The other young guards in his new salary range are Immanuel Quickley and Jalen Suggs, whose contracts don't look like bargains a couple of years after they signed. George might be a better player than them, but it would have been nice to see his development, particularly on defense, for another year before judging his pricey new deal an unreserved win for the Jazz.

Sept. 17: Bey signs extension with Pelicans
Saddiq Bey terms: Three years, $55.5 million

Grade: B

Bey arrived in New Orleans as an afterthought. The former Detroit Piston, Atlanta Hawk and Washington Wizard missed the 2024-25 season because of a torn ACL before shipping to New Orleans in the Jordan Poole-CJ McCollum swap.

Bey responded to his new circumstances with the best season of his career. He started 64 games (out of 72 total played) last season and averaged a career-high 17.7 points. He made 37% of his 3s and showed improvement as a perimeter defender.

So the Pelicans gave him a big raise, from $6.6 million in this upcoming season to an average of $18.5 million over the following three years, which will keep Bey in New Orleans through his age-30 season. That's a solid contract for a solid player.

It's a bit less clear how New Orleans plans to structure its wing rotation in the short and long term, with Bey, Bennedict Mathurin, Trey Murphy III and Herbert Jones all worthy of playing time, to say nothing of Zion Williamson and/or Derik Queen grabbing minutes at power forward.

To that end, it's possible that Bey's new contract could make New Orleans more amenable to a trade of Murphy or Jones, two more established wings who could fetch draft picks from contenders.

Sept 3: Rockets, Amen Thompson agree to five-year deal
Amen Thompson terms: Five years, $208 million

Grade: A-

Thompson is the second member of the 2023 draft class to sign a rookie extension this summer, following in the steps of No. 1 pick Victor Wembanyama. That order tracks, as Thompson is the second-best player from that draft class after Wembanyama.

He might not have exploded into superstardom as some expected -- and as Wembanyama did -- last season, but Thompson still fits the profile of a future two-way star. He's only 23 years old, he's one of the NBA's fiercest perimeter defenders and he boosted both his points (18.3 per game) and assists (5.3 per game) last season while leading the NBA in minutes played.

Thompson's 3-point shot remains a glaring hole in his game, as he's at just 22% from distance in his career on low volume. That weakness could limit his ultimate upside, as he might be best suited as an ace defender and offensive role player, rather than a No. 1 scoring option.

But given his present ability and future potential, extending him was a no-brainer for Houston. And as they have with other recent first-round picks, including Jabari Smith Jr., Alperen Sengun and the since-traded Jalen Green, the Rockets actually negotiated with Thompson to save some money, rather than simply presenting him with a max deal to sign.

Compare Thompson's new deal to Wembanyama's max contract, which is worth an estimated $252 million. The difference between the two extensions comes out to about $44 million over five years, or $8 million to $9 million per year -- which the Rockets can instead use to add an extra role player or help squeeze in other expensive players under the various tax thresholds.

Locking in that number for Thompson now also means the Rockets won't run the risk of paying even more for his new deal if he makes an All-NBA team (or wins Defensive Player of the Year or MVP) this upcoming season, which would have allowed him to qualify for rookie supermax status.

This deal thus carries tremendous benefits for both parties. Thompson gains generational wealth before he reaches his mid-20s, and the Rockets both retain their most talented young player for the long term and maintain a bit of financial flexibility in the process. That sounds like a win-win.

Aug. 26: Kuminga, Timberwolves agree on two-year deal
Jonathan Kuminga terms: Two years, $12.4 million, player option in Year 2

Grade: A-

Few players in recent memory have received more fanfare, relative to their on-court impact, than Kuminga. The former No. 7 pick was a key member of the Warriors' theoretical "two timelines" dynastic extension, and he was a main character of the 2025 offseason, as he lingered in restricted free agency.

A year later, however, Kuminga's new contract actually deserves the attention -- but more for the context of his new situation than because of his own development.

One of the main reasons that I was critical of the Timberwolves' trade for LaMelo Ball is that the series of transactions they used to acquire the All-Star point guard left them with a giant, gaping hole at power forward. They were already a top-heavy team without much depth, and then they parted with Julius Randle and Naz Reid in the process.

And with the LeBron James dream dashed last month, the Timberwolves had few remaining resources to acquire another frontcourt contributor. The Ball trade left them with almost no draft capital -- they have zero tradeable first-round picks, and their only tradeable second is a top-50-protected selection from Memphis in 2030 -- and they're hard-capped at the second apron, with only about $4 million in wiggle room below that barrier. (Thus, they will have to figure out a way to dump some salary before officially signing Kuminga.)

So given all those limitations, and the slim pickings nearly two months into free agency, Kuminga was clearly the best option available. The expectation is that he'll join Ball, Anthony Edwards, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert in a talented starting lineup, where Kuminga's ability to run the floor should get him enough easy buckets every game to keep his scoring average in double figures.

Kuminga isn't a perfect fit in his new role. His outside shooting struggles (33% on 3s in his career) could strain his partnership with Gobert on offense, and it's still an open question whether Kuminga will ever bring the consistency required of a nailed-down NBA starter. He has always shown flashes, but never for more than a few games or weeks at a time.

Yet on the other hand, Kuminga is still just 24 years old, and he clearly has potential if he can find the right situation in which to thrive; most recently, he was one of Atlanta's best players in the playoffs. According to ESPN's Shams Charania, other teams were interested in signing Kuminga to a larger contract this summer, which points to his continued desirability despite his flaws.

He doesn't need to be a star in Minnesota, either, but rather a competent role player. He may not even close games for his new team, whose five best players are probably Gobert, McDaniels and a trio of guards. But what the Timberwolves needed most of all was a capable power forward who can protect McDaniels -- one of the league's best perimeter defenders -- from sliding up to that position full time.

They found one, at a reasonable price. As long as Kuminga stays healthy -- he has appeared in only 83 combined games over the past two seasons -- and engaged, he'll provide a meaningful upgrade to a fringe title contender next season.

Aug. 26: Pels, Mathurin reach two-year deal
Bennedict Mathurin terms: Two years, $16 million, player option in second year

Grade: B+

The Pelicans are finally getting involved in the summer transaction cycle, after essentially sitting on their hands for the first two months of the offseason.

They picked their first spot well. Mathurin is still just 24 years old, with the potential befitting a former No. 6 pick. He's a strong individual scorer who averaged a career-high 17.6 PPG last year, and his driving ability and free throw generation remain standout skills.

Among all active non-centers with at least 5,000 career minutes, Mathurin ranks sixth in career free throw attempt rate (or the number of free throw attempts per field goal attempt). The rest of the top 10 is filled with superstars:

That said, Mathurin has been a one-dimensional player throughout his career, which holds him back from reaching the same overall level as those superstars. He has averaged only 1.9 assists per game, and he's a weak defender despite his 6-foot-5 frame.

It's notable that both the Pacers -- who saw Mathurin up close for four years -- and Clippers, who had him for half a season after the Ivica Zubac trade, were comfortable letting him go despite his youth and potential, and that Mathurin didn't attract other suitors as a restricted free agent.

But for this price and contract length, Mathurin's addition is a low-risk gamble for New Orleans, which is in need of more talent. (Expect further transactions before the season begins to create more space to fit Mathurin below the first apron.)

The second-year player option reduces some of the upside for the Pelicans, as they could lose Mathurin as early as next summer if he takes a leap under their purview. But they'd surely be thrilled if he made that leap in the first place.

Aug. 21: Thompson to join Heat after Mavs buyout
Klay Thompson terms: Two years, $13 million, player option in second year

Grade: B-

Thompson's on-court value no longer matches his name value, as a future Hall of Famer who was a centerpiece of the NBA's last great dynasty.

There's a reason, after all, that the Mavericks were amenable to buying Thompson out of the last year of his contract to pave his path to Miami. He is now 36 years old and nowhere near the sort of two-way star he was at his peak. Instead, the five-time All-Star is now a well below-average player.

DARKO Career DPM Progression

But Thompson will bring one important skill to Miami that the Heat are currently lacking: Even as he has declined, he has remained an elite shooter. Thompson has made at least 38% of his 3-pointers on high volume in every season of his career, and even coming off the bench last season, he ranked among the top 20 players in made 3s per game.

Incidentally, Thompson ranked second in total 3s from a reserve last season -- one spot behind Tim Hardaway Jr., his new teammate on Miami's perimeter.

Because the Heat already added Hardaway in free agency, it's possible that Thompson's presence will be redundant. And a two-year, $13 million deal with a second-year player option is less of an obvious win for Miami than a veteran minimum would have been.

But in truth, the Heat need all the shooting they can get around Giannis Antetokounmpo, after they lost Norman Powell and Tyler Herro, their top two shooters last season. And if any team can cover for Thompson on the defensive end, where he's now a liability because of his age and injury history, it might be a group with Antetokounmpo, Bam Adebayo, Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins, to say nothing of Erik Spoelstra pulling the strategic strings.

It's still unlikely that Thompson, at this stage of his career, will be a major difference-maker for his new team. But Thompson is a better use of a roster spot than other options Miami had to complete its 2026-27 rotation.

Aug. 21: DeRozan joins Nuggets on one-year deal
DeMar DeRozan terms: One year, $3.9 million

Grade: B

Presumably, DeRozan signed this contract knowing he'd likely be asked to come off the bench in Denver, even though he has started every NBA game he has played since his rookie year -- 1,250 and counting, between the regular season and playoffs.

That shift couldn't come at a better time for the Nuggets, whose bench was incredibly depleted following the Peyton Watson sign-and-trade earlier this week. This is far from a like-for-like replacement, to be clear: DeRozan is about as different from Watson as two similarly sized players can be. The 23-year-old Watson is strongest on defense and -- in a new turn -- from the 3-point line; the 37-year-old DeRozan is a midrange master with considerable defensive limitations.

That difference could make DeRozan a somewhat clunky fit in Denver, where he won't patch the defensive holes left by Watson's departure, and where his lack of 3-point range could complicate his fit with Nikola Jokic (and Christian Braun, if he can't rebound from last season's 30% performance from distance).

But on a relative basis, DeRozan should provide a major upgrade in his new home. Until the six-time All-Star joined on a veteran minimum contract, the Nuggets' highest-scoring reserves were projected as backup center Marvin Bagley III (10.5 points per game last season) and wing Julian Strawther (7.2).

Even in his late 30s, DeRozan offers a different level of scoring and playmaking -- he's a very underrated passer -- than any other option outside the Nuggets' starting lineup. He should be able to help stabilize the offense when Jokic or Jamal Murray rest, as he has continued to score efficiently even in a dour situation in Sacramento over the past two seasons.

For years now, Denver's bench has been a problem, and DeRozan won't come close to solving that issue all on his own. But it's slightly less of an issue today than it was yesterday.

Aug. 20: Harden, Cavs agree to new contract

James Harden terms: Three years, $97 million, with a player option in the third year

Grade: B

At this point, you know what you're getting with Harden. He has remained a metronomic offensive force even into his late 30s; he can create for others and score of his own accord inside, outside and at the free throw line. He also rarely misses time, as he has appeared in 70 or more games in each of the past three seasons.

That combination makes for a powerful regular-season catalyst. In 15 of his 17 NBA seasons, including each of the last 10, Harden has finished the year with a team that won at least 50 games (or the equivalent winning percentage in a shortened season). He has never finished with a losing record.

You also know, however, the downsides that come with relying on Harden. He was a relatively indifferent defender even in his 20s, and now he's one of the least active defenders in the league. His production also routinely shrinks in the postseason, or at the very least becomes wildly inconsistent.

Those attributes are essentially baked into Harden's player profile at this point, and his return to Cleveland also seemed baked in as soon as the Cavaliers traded Darius Garland for him at last season's deadline. The Clippers weren't willing to extend Harden at his desired amount, so he sought a trade to a team that would.

And after Harden declined his $42 million player option earlier this summer, it was only a matter of time before the Cavaliers completed the rest of their offseason business -- which they did with the Peyton Watson sign-and-trade on Wednesday -- and brought back Harden on a longer-term deal with a lower annual value.

The resulting contract is a year longer than would be optimal for the Cavaliers, as it gives Harden a player option in his age-39 season. A straight two-year deal in the $60 million range would have protected Cleveland more against potential decline as Harden ages.

But for all the holes in Harden's game, he's still a valuable playmaker and regular-season innings eater, and his backcourt partnership with Donovan Mitchell worked reasonably well in limited time last year. The Cavaliers certainly couldn't afford to lose him, with Garland already gone and no means to replace his production with another trade or free agent signing.

That 2028-29 player option could -- and likely will -- prove problematic in a couple of years. But the Cavaliers are an all-in, win-now team, and they're hoping that Harden helps them finally get over the playoff hump and return to the Finals at some point before then.

Aug. 13: Beal re-signs with Clippers

Bradley Beal terms: Two years, $13.2 million

Grade: C

Beal declined a $5.6 million player option in late June before agreeing to a new deal with the LA Clippers six weeks later. He didn't make much of an impression in his first stint in Los Angeles, appearing in only six games before undergoing season-ending hip surgery.

In those six games, Beal averaged a career-low 8.2 points and experienced a startling decline in efficiency and production. His player efficiency rating ranked 498th out of 503 players with at least 100 minutes played last season.

On the one hand, it would be easy to chalk up that decline to Beal's injury and expect a bounce-back performance in 2026-27. On the other hand, Beal is now 33 years old with a fairly extensive injury history -- he hasn't played more than 53 games since 2020-21 with the Washington Wizards -- and he was already on the downslope of his career in Phoenix before becoming a Clipper.

Because of that context, it's hard to expect much of anything from Beal at this point. His re-signing won't complicate the Clippers' finances, but it likely won't move the needle on the court, either.

Aug. 6: Suns sign Brooks to extension through 2030
Dillon Brooks terms: Three years, $73 million

Grade: B-

Brooks was a revelation in his first season in Phoenix, after heading to the Suns in the trade that sent Kevin Durant to Houston. Not only did the veteran wing average a career-high 20.2 points per game, but his attitude and mentality spread throughout the franchise.

"He's exactly the type of player [who fits] what we talk about here in Phoenix, what we want to be, the identity of the Suns," team owner Mat Ishbia told ESPN's Tim MacMahon earlier this year.

Phoenix is keeping him around for a few years longer, at a fairly reasonable price. Brooks is entering the last year of a four-year, $86 million contract that accounted for about 15% of the salary cap per season; his new three-year extension projects to make up about 13% of the salary cap each season until 2029-30.

From the pure perspective of his on-court value, Brooks doesn't project to be worth that much money, given his age -- this extension covers his age-32 to 34 seasons, when he'll likely be in the decline phase -- and unimpressive advanced statistics. He has never been an efficient scorer, with a below-average true shooting mark in every season of his career.

But given his cultural fit and leadership responsibilities in Phoenix -- and the fact that the rising salary cap means a $24.3 million average salary will account for such a manageable portion of it -- this extension makes a lot of sense for the Suns. It's not as team-friendly as some of Phoenix's other deals this summer, such as bringing back Collin Gillespie and Jordan Goodwin, but it might have a greater impact nonetheless because of Brooks' more prominent role on the team.

Aug. 2: Marshall, Mavericks agree to extension
Naji Marshall terms: Three years, $52.2 million

Grade: B-

Marshall was set to enter unrestricted free agency next summer but instead signed a three-year contract that will keep him with the Dallas Mavericks through the 2029-30 season. Not accounting for inflation, this extension is essentially double what he signed for two years ago, when he joined the Mavericks on a three-year, $27 million free agent contract.

He has earned a raise in that time. In his first four seasons, all with the Pelicans, Marshall never averaged more than 9.1 points, but he has averaged 13.2 and 15.2 points in his two seasons in Dallas. Marshall's rise has gone under the radar amid all the other drama surrounding the Mavericks during those years, but he has quietly blossomed into a solid NBA forward.

After that developmental leap, Marshall grades out an average player -- he scores with near-average efficiency on a near-average usage rate (20.3% in Dallas, versus an average of 20.0%), leading to a near-average player efficiency rating (15.3 in Dallas, versus an average of 15.0).

So why does an extension that will keep that caliber of player in town through the rest of his prime, for only around 10% of the salary cap, receive a mere B-minus grade rather than higher marks? Because of one key weakness in Marshall's game: He's only a 30% career 3-point shooter, and he has been even worse (28%) in Dallas.

Granted, Marshall has enjoyed considerable improvement from 2-point range, and a healthy free throw rate buoys his overall efficiency. But absent a better 3-point shot, he won't fulfill the ultimate 3-and-D potential.

If he had a more threatening jump shot, Marshall would be a surefire starter, but he's instead stuck with the profile of a fringe starter or solid bench player for a good team. That weakness also complicates his fit on a Mavericks roster with so many other questionable shooters in the frontcourt, from Cooper Flagg to 2026 lottery pick Morez Johnson Jr. to a host of paint-bound centers.

Because of its length and manageable cap figure, the Mavericks are unlikely to ever seriously regret giving Marshall this extension. But they're also unlikely to end up viewing it as a slam dunk success, either.

July 28: Draymond back to Warriors
Draymond Green terms: One year, $27.7 million

Grade: C

Before the offseason began, the expectation was that Green would play out the 2026-27 season on a $27.7 million deal. He had a player option for that amount and likely wouldn't have received any more on the open market as a 36-year-old with more value to the Golden State Warriors than any other team.

That expectation changed for about a month, after Green declined his player option to give the Warriors the financial flexibility to pursue free agent LeBron James. But after James went to Philadelphia 76ers rather than northern California, it made sense for Green to re-sign with the Warriors for the same one-year deal he declined a month earlier. Because the baseline for these free agent grades is a "C," and because Green stuck with the baseline expectation entering this summer, that's the logical grade to give this deal.

But the one-year pact, rather than a multiyear deal with a lower annual value but more total guaranteed money, sets up a fascinating situation next summer. Golden State's three highest-paid players -- Stephen Curry, Jimmy Butler III and Green -- could all enter free agency in 2027, while the fourth-highest-paid player is Kristaps Porzingis, whose deal is guaranteed for only $3 million in 2027-28.

That means Golden State could set itself up for tremendous cap space a year from now. Even a hefty new deal for Curry, who becomes extension-eligible on Aug. 29, wouldn't take up all that space.

More on the Warriors' offseason

July 24: LeBron chooses 76ers

LeBron James terms: Two years, $8 million

Grade: A+

How James fits in a new-look, star-studded lineup in Philadelphia, immediately becomes one of the most fascinating questions in the NBA.

On the one hand, James averaged 20.9 points per game last season, tied with his rookie campaign for the lowest of his career. His 27% usage rate was his lowest ever, and his time of possession was by far his lowest in the tracking era (since 2013-14): James handled the ball for 3.8 minutes per game in 2025-26, a 37% drop from his previous low of 5.3 minutes. He also averaged just 15.5 picks per 100 possessions as the ball handler, a 40% drop from his previous low.

Yet on the other hand, James was still productive and efficient by any measure, and he settled much more comfortably into a secondary offensive role -- which he'll presumably occupy once more in Philadelphia -- as the season continued. His 59% true shooting was right in line with his career average (also 59%) and his mark across eight seasons with the Lakers (60%). And he averaged 7.2 assists per game, generated gobs of free throws and played 1,989 minutes, which was the third most on the Lakers.

July 11: Bucks bring back Trent on big deal
Gary Trent Jr. terms: Four years, $64 million

Grade: D-

Half a decade ago, Trent signed a three-year, $54 million contract with Toronto. It made sense at the time: Trent was 22 years old and coming off a breakout season, during which he was traded for Norman Powell. He looked like a strong 3-and-D prospect.

On Saturday, Trent agreed to similar terms on a new deal: four years, $64 million to stay with the Bucks. But there's only one problem: He has declined significantly since his early 20s.

Trent was arguably the least valuable veteran rotation player in the entire NBA last season. He averaged only 8.1 points, 1.2 assists and 1.0 rebounds per game, and his 3-point percentage fell to a league-average 36%.

Out of 279 players with at least 1,000 minutes, Trent ranked 276th in both box plus/minus and player efficiency rating, and every player below him was 21 or younger. Trent, conversely, was an eight-year veteran in his age-27 season.

Given the combination of that decline and the Bucks' overabundance of young guards who need playing time -- after the draft and the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade -- it makes little sense for Milwaukee to lavish Trent with a new contract with so many dollars and so many years. Still in his 20s, he has time to bounce back, but for the moment, he profiles more like a minimum-salary player than one who deserves eight figures per year.

Coincidentally, Trent played on minimum or near-minimum deals for Milwaukee in each of the past two seasons, despite coming off much better performances in both years. Last summer, he signed a two year, $7.5 million deal with a second-year player option, which he declined, despite his woeful 2025-26 campaign, to secure a much larger payday this summer.

July 10: Wemby, Spurs agree on rookie extension
Victor Wembanyama terms: Five years, $252 million

Grade: A+

This might be the easiest transaction I'll ever grade.

Before last season, 83% of the NBA's general managers chose Wembanyama as the player they'd most like to build a franchise around. And that number has probably risen since, as Wembanyama was the unanimous Defensive Player of the Year, finished third in MVP voting and was the best player on a Finals team in 2025-26.

The Spurs would have received an "A" grade for extending Wembanyama no matter the contract details. He could have received the max, a player option and "Rose rule" salary escalator language, and Spurs brass would have been thrilled.

But in the end, he did not take every possible bell and whistle allowed for a player of his experience level, which boosts this grade to an "A+" for the Spurs.

According to ESPN's Shams Charania, Wembanyama is locking himself into a 25% maximum contract. He could have chosen an extension that would rise to 30% of the cap if he received postseason honors next year -- which seems like a virtual lock if Wembanyama reaches the 65-game minimum for awards consideration again.

Many other young stars have opted for that latter route in recent years, and they deserve no blame for maximizing their earnings. Evan Mobley, for instance, landed a 30% supermax before winning Defensive Player of the Year in 2025.

But Wembanyama has evidently taken a lesson from the star guard who beat the Spurs in the Finals last month, after the Knicks' title run was aided in part by Jalen Brunson's decision to sacrifice some of his own potential earnings to help New York build a championship roster.

The difference between 25% and 30% of the cap projects as $8.7 million next season, per ESPN's Bobby Marks, and that gap would grow over the course of Wembanyama's extension to a total of $50 million over five years.
